title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
date_evidence: meta-eli:date_document: 2026-07-08; meta-eli:first_date_entry_in_force: 2026-07-27; document title carries "of 8 July 2026"
key_claim: The Digital Omnibus on AI is a regulation of 8 July 2026 amending the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) together with the EASA Regulation and the Machinery Regulation, framed as simplification of the implementation of harmonised AI rules. It entered into force on 27 July 2026.
frame_summary: The co-legislators are presenting the instrument as a simplification of implementation rather than a reopening of the AI Act's substance, which is what allows a governance change of this size to travel inside a package titled simplification.
verbatim_quote: as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence
verbatim_list: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026

title: AI Omnibus enters into force
date_evidence: On-page item metadata: "NEWS ARTICLE / Publication 27 July 2026"; last update 31 July 2026
key_claim: The Commission's own summary of the AI Omnibus groups the changes under innovation support, extended timelines, reduced administrative burdens, safety and fundamental rights, and AI governance alignment. Under governance it records extended enforcement powers for the AI Office over certain AI systems, including those built on general-purpose models and embedded in large online platforms and search engines, alongside the deferral of Annex III high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 and Annex I rules to 2 August 2028.
frame_summary: The Commission is arguing that the Omnibus is a proportionate simplification that preserves safeguards, with the enlargement of the AI Office's oversight presented as governance alignment rather than as a transfer of enforcement authority.
verbatim_quote: The AI Office will have extended oversight of certain AI systems, including those built on general-purpose models and embedded in large online platforms and search engines
verbatim_list: High-risk AI systems in Annex III: Rules apply starting 2 December 2027
High-risk AI embedded in physical products (machinery, toys, lifts, etc.) in Annex I: Rules apply starting 2 August 2028
On 27 July 2026, the AI Omnibus enters into force across the EU, bringing extended timelines to administrative simplification.

title: Commission starts enforcing AI Act rules and new transparency requirements on 2 August
date_evidence: On-page item metadata: "PRESS RELEASE / Publication 31 July 2026"; last update 31 July 2026
key_claim: From 2 August 2026 the Commission's AI Office, together with national authorities, begins enforcing the AI Act, and the Article 50 transparency rules start to apply. The Commission published a first list of more than 180 organisations that signed the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content, and points readers to an AI Act complaints tool, an AI Act whistleblower tool and a complaints channel for downstream providers using general-purpose AI models, all operated centrally.
frame_summary: The Commission is arguing that enforcement of the AI Act has begun in a shared mode with national authorities, while in practice presenting Brussels-operated complaint, whistleblower and downstream-provider channels as the route by which enforcement matters reach a regulator.
verbatim_quote: From 2 August 2026, the European Commission's AI Office, together with national authorities, will begin enforcing the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act.
verbatim_list: The Commission published a first list of more than 180 organisations that have signed the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content
Deepfakes (images, videos, or audio that have been edited or generated using AI) will have to be labelled.

title: Marktüberwachung (market surveillance under the AI Regulation)
key_claim: Germany's designated AI market surveillance authority sets out its role under Article 70 of the AI Regulation. For Annex I harmonised areas such as medical devices, machinery and radio equipment, existing market surveillance structures are to be relied on, and the Bundesnetzagentur already holds competence for radio equipment under Directive 2014/53/EU. For the Article 43(1) and Annex III areas, which include critical infrastructure and law enforcement, the page states that no market surveillance structures have existed to date and that the tasks are to be concentrated centrally at the Bundesnetzagentur.
frame_summary: The German regulator is arguing that national AI market surveillance has to be built rather than reassigned, because for the Annex III high-risk domains there is no existing supervisory apparatus to inherit.
verbatim_quote: In diesen Bereichen gibt es bisher keine Strukturen der Marktüberwachung.
verbatim_list: Hier sollen die Aufgaben der Marktüberwachung künftig bei der Bundesnetzagentur an zentraler Stelle gebündelt werden.

title: How Much Power Does the EU AI Office Actually Have?
date_evidence: On-page byline: "Monday, May 18, 2026, 1:00 PM"; meta-citation_date: 5/18/2026 5:00:03 PM
key_claim: From 2 August 2026 the AI Office gains three graduated powers over general-purpose AI model providers: Article 91 information and documentation requests, Article 92 evaluations including access through APIs or other technical means and source code, and Article 93 requested measures up to restriction, withdrawal or recall, with an Article 93(3) commitments mechanism modelled on EU competition law. Article 101 sets the maximum fine at 3% of worldwide annual turnover or €15 million, whichever is higher, imposed by the Commission directly rather than by national regulators. Christoph notes the Office is significantly under-resourced relative to its mandate, cites Pour Demain's recommendation to scale GPAI supervisory capacity to at least 160 staff by 2030, and observes that the Omnibus grants the Office exclusive supervisory authority over AI systems built on GPAI models where model and system share a provider and over systems in very large online platforms.
frame_summary: Lawfare is arguing that the AI Office now holds among the most far-reaching regulatory powers any government has claimed over frontier AI, and that the binding uncertainty is not the legal authority but whether the Office has the staff, the evaluators and the appetite to use it in its first enforcement year.
verbatim_quote: through APIs or other technical means, including source code
verbatim_list: The maximum fine is 3 percent of the provider's total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year, or 15 million euros, whichever is higher.
Fines on GPAI model providers are imposed by the commission directly, rather than by national regulators.

It grants the office exclusive supervisory authority over AI systems built on GPAI models where the model and system are developed by the same provider, and over AI systems that constitute or are integrated into very large online platforms under the DSA.
The AI Office, by contrast, is significantly underresourced relative to its mandate.
recommended scaling the GPAI supervisory capacity to at least 160 staff by 2030

title: EU AI Act Omnibus Agreement: Postponed High-Risk Deadlines and Other Key Changes
key_claim: The canonical legal account of what the trilogue deal contains. High-risk obligations deferred to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I) with fixed dates replacing the conditional trigger; a new Article 5 prohibition on nudification tools and CSAM with a transitional period to 2 December 2026; the Commission empowered to limit the application of specific AI Act requirements where sectoral legislation imposes equivalent obligations; and the AI Office given exclusive competence over AI systems built on GPAI models by the same provider and over systems integrated into VLOPs and VLOSEs, equipped with powers to conduct investigations and on-site inspections, accept binding commitments and impose fines, while national authorities remain competent for law enforcement, border management, judicial authorities and financial institutions.
frame_summary: Gibson Dunn is arguing that the Omnibus is a deferral rather than a dismantling, with the AI Act's architecture intact, and treats the reinforcement of the AI Office's supervisory role as a clarification rather than as the principal change in the package.
verbatim_quote: The AI Office is also equipped with new enforcement tools, including powers to conduct investigations and on-site inspections, accept binding commitments, and impose fines.
verbatim_list: The AI Office is given exclusive competence over AI systems built on general-purpose AI (GPAI) models where the model and the system are developed by the same provider, as well as over AI systems integrated into VLOPs/VLOSEs under the Digital Services Act.
National authorities remain competent for law enforcement, border management, judicial authorities, and financial institutions.
The Commission is empowered to limit the application of specific AI Act requirements where sectoral legislation already imposes equivalent obligations.
It is, however, a deferral rather than a dismantling

title: Loss of control: closing the governance gap before the first incident
date_evidence: On-page byline block above the article: "Jul 1" with "11 min read", on a 2026 post index; the piece cites the International AI Safety Report 2026 and an Economist leader of 7 May 2026
key_claim: Pour Demain argues that the AI Act's general-purpose AI provisions are built around placing on the market and putting into service, so internal deployment of frontier models at the labs that build them may fall outside the AI Office's Safety Unit A3 mandate. Its fifth recommendation is to resource the Office accordingly: its separate analysis estimates the unit requires a minimum of 160 staff by 2030 and an annual budget of €50 million to €60 million to match the supervisory demands of GPAI enforcement.
frame_summary: Pour Demain is arguing that Europe has assigned the AI Office a mandate that is simultaneously too narrow in scope and too large for its resources, so the governance gap that matters is the distance between the Office's legal authority and its operating capacity.
verbatim_quote: estimates that Safety Unit A3 requires a minimum of 160 staff by 2030 and an annual budget in the range of €50–60 million to match the supervisory demands of GPAI enforcement
verbatim_list: 160 staff by 2030
€50–60 million
If the AI Office is to supervise internal deployment of frontier models in addition to its existing mandate, it will need commensurate capacity.
notes: Policy institute with a stated position on AI governance; treated directionally and used only for the capacity argument, which is a recommendation rather than a finding. title: Overview of all AI Act National Implementation Plans
date_evidence: On-page italic line at the head of the article: "Last update: 17 June 2026" (original post 08 Nov, 2024)
key_claim: Member States had until 2 August 2025 to designate a market surveillance authority and a notifying authority. As of 17 June 2026, 9 Member States had designated both ('clear'), 12 had pending legislative proposals, announcements or one appointed authority ('partial clarity'), and 6 had designated or established no competent authority ('unclear'). All 27 have designated fundamental rights authorities under Article 77. Germany's draft AI market surveillance law, adopted by the Federal Cabinet on 10 February 2026, would designate the Bundesnetzagentur, and had still to pass the Bundestag and Bundesrat at the time of the update.
frame_summary: The tracker is arguing that national implementation of the AI Act remains substantially incomplete more than ten months past the designation deadline, and that the variation between centralised and decentralised national models will itself shape how the Act is enforced.
verbatim_quote: 9 Member States have designated both market surveillance and notifying authorities
verbatim_list: To our knowledge, 12 Member States have pending legislative proposals, made announcements or have appointed one competent authority
whereas 6 Member States have yet to designate or establish any competent authority
Member States had until 2 August 2025 to establish or designate a market surveillance authority and a notifying authority. Many Member States failed to meet the deadline.
At the date of this post, all EU Member States have already designated their fundamental rights authorities.
